entries.title: Beginning Middle End by Valeria Luiselli review – a mother and daughter’s odyssey
entries.summary: This journey of discovery from the US to Sicily tackles urgent themes, but is increasingly inward-lookingIn Grace Paley’s short story A Conversation With My Father, a request is made of the Paley-like narrator. “I would like you to write a simple story just once more,” her father says, “the kind Maupassant wrote, or Chekhov … Just recognisable people and then write down what happened to them next.
entries.content:
In Grace Paley’s short story A Conversation With My Father, a request is made of the Paley-like narrator. “I would like you to write a simple story just once more,” her father says, “the kind Maupassant wrote, or Chekhov … Just recognisable people and then write down what happened to them next.” Her attempt, and its failure to impress him, is the action that powers the story. Valeria Luiselli’s fourth novel is propelled by a similar request, the daughter of the Luiselli-like narrator asking: “Will you finally write a novel with a beginning, a middle, and an end?” It’s a problem Luiselli has addressed before. In her 2017 book-length essay about undocumented migrant children, Tell Me How It Ends, she writes that the difficulty in telling their story “is that it has no beginning, no middle and no end”.

Beginning Middle End charts the narrator’s efforts to corral life into a narrative. The father in Paley’s story would be similarly unimpressed. After a “slow, entangled” divorce, the narrator, a Mexican living in the United States, embarks on a European book tour with her 12-year-old daughter. She has a coil removed in Munich; her daughter loses a tooth in Prague; near Amsterdam they watch children learning to swim with their shoes on in case of floods. When summer comes, the pair fly to Catania in Sicily. The narrator’s grandmother grew up nearby. They stay in the apartment of a pianist who’s away on tour, with whom the narrator had a “brief and feverish encounter” the previous year.

This book can be made to sound dense with plot: Etna is erupting. Wildfires rage. The narrator’s mother, in Baja California, might be developing dementia and is possibly planning an act of eco-terrorism. Before the narrator left for Europe her mother gave her a valuable heirloom, a Roman mosaic tile portraying the god Proteus; the narrator’s grandmother took it from an excavation site before leaving Sicily.

Mother and daughter discuss Proteus’s appearance in the Odyssey, their explorations of myth and classical literature becoming a central strand. The narrator’s daughter grows obsessed with returning the mosaic to the ruined villa it came from.

After a few weeks the pianist returns, the narrator’s attraction to him rapidly eroding as the sex gets rough, he fights with her daughter, and neglects to help when she gets stung by jellyfish. Yet despite all this, the novel has trouble gathering momentum – or perhaps isn’t interested in doing so. Paley’s narrator calls plot “the absolute line between two points which I’ve always despised”. Luiselli’s seems to feel the same way, breaking her narrative into discrete little segments like the tesserae from which Proteus’s face emerges.

Throughout, the narrator questions what she is writing. “I don’t have a clear idea about what I am doing, or what will happen next, not yet,” she admits. “I get entangled in possible beginnings, intricate plots, improvised premises.” Later she wonders if this project isn’t a novel at all but an essay. “Perhaps the middle does not fit into the tighter architecture of a novel, the corset of plot. The middle feels more akin to the distracted, loose, meandering spirit of essaying. Maybe it will have to be an essay until it can be a novel again, an essay with a beginning, a middle, and an end.” This persistent identity crisis is only resolved when the daughter eventually seizes control of the narrative.

Luiselli’s writing has always been essayistic and self-reflexive. In fact, she began in 2010 as an essayist with the lyrical, literary Sidewalks. Her first novel, Faces in the Crowd, blended autofiction and metafiction – the book portraying its own construction, just as Beginning Middle End does – with a fictionalised account of the life of a real Mexican poet. Her second, The Story of My Teeth, is also partly about its own construction: in an author’s note Luiselli explains how the book was created in tandem with a group of factory workers. In a Sebaldian touch, photographs accompany the text.

In many ways Beginning Middle End mirrors Luiselli’s previous novel, 2019’s Lost Children Archive, itself a fictional expansion of Tell Me How It Ends. Its narration is shared between an unnamed woman, whose marriage is collapsing, and her stepson, who addresses his part to his stepsister. In Beginning Middle End the unnamed narrator’s marriage has ended, and her daughter writes postcards to her stepbrother. In both books the text is divided into short, titled chapters that prefer essayistic thought to the construction of dramatic scenes. Both children come into possession of Polaroid cameras, their pictures providing wordless conclusions to each novel. There is another explicit link, one that paradoxically divides the books’ narrators, but revealing it would be a spoiler.

The larger contradiction within Luiselli’s work is that although the subjects it returns to – the role and status of the mother, migration, the climate crisis – are universal and urgent, it is becoming ever more inward-looking. The most dramatic journey Beginning Middle End describes is whether it can succeed in becoming the book we hold in our hands. In a knowing moment, the narrator’s daughter studies the mosaic of Proteus – a shapeshifter, just like this novel – “as if she were looking into a mirror or a pool of water, like a little Narcissus peering at himself”. Since finishing the book, it’s the image that has persisted most strongly in my memory.

entries.title: Alive by Melanie Challenger review – a maverick study of what it means to have a body
entries.summary: In this disorienting book, a poet argues we have been looking at nature – and ourselves – the wrong wayThe eastern breakwater of Granton harbour is almost 1km long, and swimmers can follow its crooked finger, heading straight out into the Firth of Forth, while benefiting from its reassuring presence. One Thursday lunchtime, I thought: why not, let’s give it a go, and headed for its tip. I felt col
entries.content:
The eastern breakwater of Granton harbour is almost 1km long, and swimmers can follow its crooked finger, heading straight out into the Firth of Forth, while benefiting from its reassuring presence. One Thursday lunchtime, I thought: why not, let’s give it a go, and headed for its tip. I felt cold, but, as I progressed, I seemed to grow strangely warmer. I did not notice the complaints from my body: the creeping numbness which proceeded from my fingers to my elbow, nor the coldness of my pee. Only by the time I exited the water, club footed and claw handed, did it hit me that I was hypothermic.

The irony of this reckless exercise was that in my swim bag there was a book by Melanie Challenger called Alive: The Hidden Intelligence of the Living World. It’s an ambitious examination of the wisdom of bodies, a rhizomatic guide not just to our own, but also all the living forms around us: from bacteria to chimps. Her case is that we have ignored or misread the agency and purpose of bodies to our detriment; in a way it is a plea to listen to them. I wish I had read it before my ill-advised swim.

Challenger notes that her book was born out of “wild curiosity”, and a sense that the “stories we were telling ourselves … were both presumptuous and unconvincing”. For her, our focus on souls, genes or minds is a distortion of reality, and we should instead direct our attention to our bodies, which have been marginalised, perhaps because they remind us of our own vulnerability and mortality. It is not that Challenger denies the importance of genes; what she questions is the lens through which we read the world.

Throughout the book she vividly presents a range of different organisms, from slime to squid, exploring the ways in which they relate and respond to the world around them. Among other things, Challenger is a poet, and her descriptions are often beautiful. She describes glacial ice as “blue sheened like an eyeball” and a Humboldt squid as “a lozenge of silver”. By denigrating or ignoring bodies, she argues, we are blinded to the sophistication of other life forms, and do not afford them the respect that they deserve; we mistake machines for consciousness and our own consciousness for machines; we destroy habitats with little regard for the non-human life that resides there.

Challenger cites an encyclopaedic range of scientists and philosophers, but her own intellectual guide is Aristotle (she thanks him in the acknowledgments). According to her, it was Aristotle who first grasped the intelligence of bodies, though he lacked the science to support his intuitions. She brings him to life at several points in the book, entering into his head, and turning the philosopher – this figure based on a collection of texts, translations, and commentaries – into flesh and bone.

I struggle to think of a book for whose subject I have felt more sympathy and excitement: its turn to the body, its trenchant critique of scientific reductionism and misguided metaphors. But as a lay reader I often found myself disoriented, almost dizzied, by the text. I desperately wanted to follow my guide, but I kept on feeling lost, left behind, as the author charged into a dense thicket of ideas and scientific research. This is perhaps the risk run by any pioneer: you can cross a frontier, but can you bring others with you?

When I got out of the water, corpse-grey and shaken, I was greeted by two concerned women, experienced swimmers in dry-robes, who kept an eye on me, and offered me a cup of tea and some sound guidance. I’m grateful to them and the way they could quietly read their own bodies, and mine, skilfully relating them to world around us. In a way this book is an invitation to the reader to do something similar; to abandon the harmful readings that we have inherited, and sidestep our own self-destruction.

entries.title: Previous winners Douglas Stuart and Marlon James lead Booker prize longlist
entries.summary: Chair of judges Mary Beard said each of the 13 books in contention for the £50,000 award ‘takes the reader to new places’Comment: This Booker longlist may have two previous winners, but it’s keen to experimentDouglas Stuart and Marlon James, two previous winners of the Booker, have been named on this year’s longlist, alongside three-time nominee Elizabeth Strout, in a collection that “rewards risk
entries.content:
Douglas Stuart and Marlon James, two previous winners of the Booker, have been named on this year’s longlist, alongside three-time nominee Elizabeth Strout, in a collection that “rewards risk”.

The 13 novels selected for the 2026 prize, announced on Tuesday, feature authors of seven nationalities across three continents, with almost half from the UK. Ten of the writers are appearing on a Booker longlist for the first time, including three debut novelists: Kenan Orhan, Rebecca Perry and Djamel White.

Chairing this year’s judging panel is the classicist and broadcaster Mary Beard, who is joined on the panel by Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker.

Beard said that each book on the longlist “brilliantly musters the power of words on the page to take the reader to new places, to see old places from new angles, to change minds.

“I would not be telling the truth if I said that I hadn’t occasionally felt daunted, as a new box of 30 or so gleaming volumes landed on my doorstep,” she added.

James is longlisted for his fifth novel, The Disappearers, based around a homophobic mob attack in 1980s Jamaica, to be published in September. The judges called it “a reckoning” from “a singular literary talent”. James won the prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings. Stuart, who won in 2020 with his debut, Shuggie Bain, returns with his third novel, John of John, which the judges praised for its “rich, textural detail”. Should either win again, they would become only the fifth author to take the Booker twice, joining JM Coetzee, Peter Carey, Hilary Mantel and Margaret Atwood.

Strout, meanwhile, picks up her third Booker nomination for The Things We Never Say, her critically acclaimed 11th novel, which reckons with Trump’s America. Strout was longlisted in 2016 for My Name Is Lucy Barton and shortlisted in 2022 for Oh William!

Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said the judges’ “range of tastes” and “openness of mind” had produced a list that “shows how capacious an art form the novel is”, adding that it “rewards risk” and contains “genuinely original work”.

The list also opens the door to two firsts. Chloe Aridjis, who is Mexican-British and longlisted for The Shadow of the Object, could become the first winner of Mexican heritage with her “mysterious and free-wheeling novel”. Kenan Orhan, Turkish-American and longlisted for his debut novel The Renovation, in which a woman discovers that her bathroom has become a prison cell, could become the first of Turkish heritage.

At 81, M John Harrison is the oldest on the list, longlisted for the first time for The End of Everything after 12 previous novels and a stint as a Booker judge himself in 2022. Should he go on to win, he would surpass Atwood as the prize’s oldest ever recipient (she was 79 when she jointly won in 2019). At the other end of the list is 28-year-old Djamel White, the only Irish writer on the list, whose debut, All Them Dogs, grew out of a short story and is set in the “criminal badlands” of west Dublin.

A total of 163 books were submitted, all written in English and published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.

Joining Beard and Cocker on the judging panel are writer Raymond Antrobus, Booker prize-shortlisted novelist, poet and essayist Patricia Lockwood, and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu. Cocker follows in the footsteps of others in the entertainment industry who have judged the prize in recent years, including Sarah Jessica Parker, Adjoa Andoh and Robert Webb.

“I was aware that I was, shall we say, the least formally qualified person on this jury, but I didn’t really let that bother me,” Cocker said in an interview. “Knowing that the Booker prizes tend to create panels including people who aren’t necessarily part of the literary world – but can read! – helped me, and I thought I was obviously supposed to bring something that others don’t: a different perspective.”

The list also includes Emma Cline’s Switzy, out in September, which tells the story of a man’s final journey to a euthanasia clinic in Zurich; Luke Kennard’s Black Bag, a comedy about a struggling actor; Rebecca Perry’s May We Feed the King, which has already won the 2026 Waterstones debut fiction prize; Gwendoline Riley’s The Palm House, a portrait of literary London; and Missouri Williams’s The Vivisectors, billed as an antidote to the “cosy campus novel”.

The shortlist will be announced at the Southbank Centre in London on 22 September, with the winner named at a ceremony on 9 November.

Last year’s winner was David Szalay’s Flesh. Other recent winners include Samantha Harvey, Paul Lynch, Shehan Karunatilaka and Damon Galgut.

entries.title: This Booker longlist may have two previous winners, but it’s keen to experiment
entries.summary: Marlon James, Douglas Stuart and Elizabeth Strout are names we know, but there’s a welcome element of surprise elsewhere Previous winners Douglas Stuart and Marlon James lead Booker prize longlistThis year’s Booker longlist is led by two previous winners. Twelve years on from A Brief History of Seven Killings, Marlon James returns to Jamaica in The Disappearers, out in September: a polyphonic epic
entries.content:
This year’s Booker longlist is led by two previous winners. Twelve years on from A Brief History of Seven Killings, Marlon James returns to Jamaica in The Disappearers, out in September: a polyphonic epic of a murderous mob attack on a gay theatre group in 1988 Kingston, and the two-decade aftermath of trauma and revenge that follows. A brutal expose of Jamaica’s homophobia, it’s also an energetic portrait of queer culture and the Caribbean diaspora. Douglas Stuart, whose debut Shuggie Bain won in 2020, is included for John of John, in which a young gay man returns to his childhood home on the Hebridean island of Harris, where his devout father is also hiding his sexuality. Both novels open up territory not often trod in literature, with Stuart illuminating faith, repression and the fading traditions of the Scottish Hebrides.

It’s no surprise either to see a third nomination for Elizabeth Strout. The Things We Never Say introduces new characters to her fictional universe, in the story of a fiftysomething teacher with a secret in his marriage and a sadness in his heart. Strout has always been interested in class and deprivation in American society; the spectre of Trump brings a growing darkness, but as ever her spiky warmth and wisdom carry the reader through. The other big-name American author on the list is Emma Cline; Switzy, out in September, takes us inside the mind of a high flyer whose grip on the world is failing as dementia encroaches. David is taking his last journey, to a euthanasia clinic in Zurich, and on the way will hopefully make his final reckonings with friends and family while he can still recognise them. It’s a technical tour de force of the unreliable narrator, and a hugely moving account of life’s meaning as everything is stripped away.

This year’s big omission is also American: Ben Lerner was widely seen as a shoo-in for Transcription, his compact but intricately allusive meditation on family inheritance, technology and the effect of smartphones on the way we see the world. But there will be rejoicing at a nomination at last for British author Gwendoline Riley, who has been writing devastatingly precise indictments of family relationships and emotional narcissism for a quarter of a century. The Palm House finds her in a more tender mood, investigating a long friendship against the precarity of London life.

It’s fantastic too to see M John Harrison’s The End of Everything, a fabulously destabilising vision of an England drifting through alien invasion into terminal decline. Harrison, who has been called “the missing evolutionary link between William Burroughs and Virginia Woolf”, began his career in the late 1960s as part of the science fiction New Wave, and has been subverting genre and perspective in steely modernist sentences ever since. This portrait of apocalypse-at-a-remove, with wars in the distance, reality bending, new forms of intelligence on the rise while humans dissociate and muddle confusedly through, perhaps speaks more to our times than realism ever could.

Indeed judge Patricia Lockwood, known for her own dazzlingly idiosyncratic prose, claimed in an interview with the Observer that “in the face of AI and the fractured attention span, I think we’re going to see a new avant garde that insists on the participation of the human … there is a new, weird literature emerging”. She jokingly threatened to choose “the craziest book on﻿ Earth!” And there’s certainly a weird and wild undercurrent in this year’s list, soaked through with absurdism and surrealism.

If one theme is the journey from margins to mainstream, it’s been a rapid progression for Missouri Williams, only on her second novel after cult success The Doloriad. Set in a university town overrun by vegetation, The Vivisectors is a deeply strange parable of culture wars, family dysfunction and civilisational decline, and an even stranger love story. “At the centre of my soul there was a big dead rock that wanted nothing to do with anything else,” says our young antiheroine, and while there are echoes of Ottessa Moshfegh here, Williams has a vision and energy all her own.

Rebecca Perry’s debut May We Feed the King is similarly uncategorisable, contrasting a contemporary narrative about a curator who recreates furnishings and feasts in historic houses with the story of an unwilling medieval ruler. It’s a puzzle box of a novel that toys with the reader but keeps them rapt throughout. American Makenna Goodman’s Helen of Nowhere is more unusual still: organised as a series of dramatic scenes, it is a witty fable of male entitlement based around a university professor whose status is upended by the changing zeitgeist. Like The Vivisectors, it’s interested in nature v civilisation, culture wars and identity politics.

“History repeats itself so fast in Turkey, faster than in any other country.” Kenan Orhan’s The Renovation uses a Kafkaesque absurdity – a bathroom in an Italian flat that suddenly becomes a prison cell in Istanbul – to open up a story about migration, home and political repression, in which the trials of loss and memory extend to the narrator’s father’s dementia. Even Luke Kennard’s comic romp Black Bag is tinged with absurdism. Here a failing actor who has “measured out my life in coffees I cannot technically afford” takes part in a university experiment, hanging around campus dressed only in a black leather bag: his parents appear as stone menhirs, and his best conversations are with a dog. Full of zinging one-liners, this is a very funny take on work, friendship, masculinity and other modern confusions.

Irish author Djamel White’s debut All Them Dogs, a tale of drug deals, bad choices and queer desire in the ganglands of Dublin, has a similarly riotous energy, while the Mexican-British author Chloe Aridjis’s The Shadow of the Object is a quieter, almost dreamlike story of a woman drawn into a fascination with magic lanterns and the technology of illusion; the ruminative mood is reminiscent of WG Sebald. The shortlist, released on 22 September, may have a different emphasis, but for the moment this is a longlist that’s eager to experiment.

entries.title: ‘We’ve always been wary of working together’: Val McDermid and Jo Sharp on writing a novel as a couple
entries.summary: The bestselling crime writer and Scotland’s first female Geographer Royal had long kept their work separate, until a chance discovery about a doomed 17th-century expedition forced them to collaborateThe airy, modern house on the outskirts of Edinburgh shared by Val McDermid and Jo Sharp is surrounded by greenery and feels as though it was designed to provide enough space for two minds to think.Bot
entries.content:
The airy, modern house on the outskirts of Edinburgh shared by Val McDermid and Jo Sharp is surrounded by greenery and feels as though it was designed to provide enough space for two minds to think.

Both women are high achievers in their fields, a Scottish power couple made up of the Queen of Crime and the Scottish Geographer Royal. Happily for them, there is normally no overlap in their work.

“We’d always been very wary of working together because we’d quite like to stay together,” says Sharp wryly. She looks at her partner of 13 years. “You don’t generally like to work with others.”

McDermid responds: “No, my mother always used to say I don’t play well with others. She wasn’t far wrong.”

McDermid’s mother would have to admit that This Door of the Seas – the couple’s jointly written novella, published next week – is an exception. The book is a fictionalised account of the 1698 Darien venture, in which more than 2,000 Scots, mostly fleeing famine, embarked on an ill-fated expedition to modern-day Panama, hoping to establish a trading colony and provide an overland route between the Atlantic and Pacific.

It is no spoiler to reveal that the attempt bankrupted a struggling Scottish economy, hampered already by its overbearing neighbour, England. It propelled the country into signing the union agreement only seven years later, taking away Scotland’s parliament, its trading company and much of its pride.

From then on, Scotland became an intrinsic part of the union, including the later evils of transatlantic slavery, a role that can sometimes go unacknowledged north of the border.

Sharp says: “One of the things that we talked about a lot is that we didn’t want to be part of what is, I think, a bit of a whitewashing of Scotland’s history, to make us seem somehow not as culpable in terms of empire and around issues of race and racism.”

Sharp is a human geographer, with a background in geopolitics and international development. She is a professor of geography at the University of St Andrews, a member of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, and became Scotland’s first female Geographer Royal in 2022.

Her civil partner, McDermid, has written 51 books, which have been translated into more than 40 languages, sold more than 20m copies and won a wealth of awards.

At 71, nearly four decades after her debut, Report for Murder, followed by immensely popular crime series including the Tony Hill and Carol Jordan books, and the Karen Pirie novels, she continues to run rings around her readers, laying breadcrumbs and pulling rugs.

The story came about through research Sharp was doing for a book festival talk. She was asked to speak about geography in Scotland, which she thought could be “quite dull”, and instead began researching the first Geographer Royal, who turned out to be “a really interesting character”.

“I discovered that shortly after he was appointed, Scotland had this endeavour to set up a trading colony in Panama, and although he didn’t go himself, he sent someone to be his eyes and ears on the ground. I just found this fascinating, because it was a bit of history I had not heard about.”

“I was telling Val all the things I’d found out about it and I said, ‘It would make a brilliant story, I just wish I could write it’,” says Sharp. “And Val then said, ‘maybe we should write it together,’ and before she got to the end of the sentence I had said yes.”

McDermid says: “My experience of writing books that have elements of historical significance in them is that what you want is something that’s got enough information to hang a story on but enough gaps to colour in.”

The aim is for the book to be “charmingly plausible”, a compliment once given to one of her historical novels. “That has been my watchword ever since. Make it charmingly plausible. Get the historical facts right and then colour in the bits around it.”

The story is told by Dr James Wallace, a scientist, in letters to his wife, Eliza, and his sponsor, Sir Robert Sibbald, the first Geographer Royal of Scotland, founder of the Edinburgh botanic gardens and physician to the king.

Sharp and McDermid worked on the structure during a rainy car journey back to Edinburgh. McDermid recalls: “You said, ‘how do we do this?’ and I said, ‘we’ll make it an epistolary novel’, and I had to explain what that was.” (“That’s not true!” interjects Sharp.)

“I was convinced someone might have had this idea already because the more excited I got about it the more I thought, surely someone’s thought about this,” says Sharp. The book felt like a good addition to the publisher Birlinn’s Darkland Tales series – reimaginings of Scottish historical and folk tales by different authors – for which McDermid had already contributed the Shakespeare retelling Queen Macbeth.

“Now the slight complication with all of this,” says Sharp, “is that about two months later, Val went in for open-heart surgery –”

“– Which I hadn’t entirely anticipated,” McDermid adds. She needed an aortic valve replacement and two coronary bypasses to fix a condition spotted initially by her partner, who noticed her heart was skipping a beat.

Sharp continues: “But the advantage of that was that I’d taken time off work to look after Val in her recovery, and there was only so much time I could wander around in my nurse’s uniform.”

Sharp did the vast majority of the research – hunting down documents including letters and ship manifests at the National Library of Scotland – while McDermid was recovering, but the pair worked together on the writing, taking turns to write and then edit each other’s work.

Slowly they began to unpick many of the myths about the Darien venture being a bumbling attempt from Scotland to stand on its own two feet, many of which Sharp realised had come not from factual accounts at the time but from political pamphlets.

The truth was the landscape was considerably harder to navigate than they had been led to believe – the colony unexpectedly came under relentless attack from the Spanish settlers who occupied territory nearby, and more than 80% of the Scots who had travelled over died within a year, mostly from tropical diseases or famine.

“People also don’t understand that nations all around Europe were setting up colonies – nine out of 10 failed,” says McDermid. “So this wasn’t that only the Scots failed, everybody failed and everybody failed a lot.”

Sharp adds: “It feeds into that story that Scotland just isn’t good enough to go alone, that we need that support of a bigger neighbour and all that kind of stuff.”

The couple have worked together once before, editing an anthology, Imagine a Country, in which Scottish writers lay out their vision for a better future. With contributors including Alan Cumming, Ali Smith, Carol Ann Duffy, Ian Rankin and Alexander McCall Smith, the collection came six years after the Scottish independence referendum, in a nation still struggling to heal from some of the divisiveness of the campaign. It was not a political book, but the pair are strong supporters of Scottish independence, believing Scotland should be given a chance to succeed on its own merits.

This Door of the Seas is more explicitly political: as the creeping sensation of betrayal by the English and Scottish landed gentry takes over, Wallace’s outrage seems to come freely to the book’s modern writers. It is a multi-generational bruise that lingers for many Scottish people more than 300 years later.

Readers will undoubtedly find similarities between those fleeing Scottish famine in the 1600s and modern refugees, many of whom do not fully comprehend the danger of the journey or the hostile environment they will be arriving in. The couple recognise the parallel.

“When the country that you’re living in offers you no hope,” says McDermid, “then the slenderest strands of hope you grasp, even if it’s not rooted in a reality.”

entries.title: Upland by Ed Douglas review – a glorious survey of Britain’s high places
entries.summary: The writer and climber brings colour and carnival to his account of a country and people shaped by its mountainsIt comes as a shock to learn that Britain’s uplands were not always rocky, covered with coarse grass and suitable only for sheep. entries.content:
It comes as a shock to learn that Britain’s uplands were not always rocky, covered with coarse grass and suitable only for sheep. About 54,000 years ago – a mere blink in geological time – this island’s high places were teeming with nature. Lushly forested peaks, crags and gorges were home to megafauna including mammoth, woolly rhinoceros and giant elk. The one sour note in this elevated Garden of Eden was the carnivorous cave lions and sabre-tooth cats who prowled the browse looking for a meaty dinner.

Ed Douglas’s achievement in this excellent book is to return a proper sense of colour and even carnival to Britain’s high places. His first job, though, is to define his terms. In 1936, the celebrated US geographer Roderick Peattie declared that what made a mountain was not its elevation so much as its capacity to “enter into the imagination of the people who lived in [its] shadows”. But by the 1990s, the United Nations, newly tasked with protecting the world’s high places from environmental and economic decline, insisted on getting out its tape measure and statistical charts and coming up with some universal criteria.

Consequently, the current definition of a “mountainous” region is one where the altitude varies by at least 300 metres over a radius of 7km. That means that Douglas’s home on Totley Moor, which sits on the millstone grit uplands of the eastern Peak District, just about qualifies; a matter of obvious satisfaction to this one-time editor of the Alpine Journal. Romping comfortably across the line are whole swathes of Scotland, Wales and northern England, not forgetting the twin domes of Exmoor and Dartmoor.

Less pleasing to Douglas, though, is the way in which Britain’s uplands have historically been imagined as places apart, spectacular yet oddly detached from life at lower levels. He reminds us that the country’s high places provide more than 60% of the nation’s water needs. What’s more, the plants that make up much of our diet originate in that same hardy environment: potatoes, barley, maize, apples, tomatoes. Those of us who live at sea level or below would do well to reformulate our ideas about the uplands as a place where nothing much grows beyond the occasional sprig of lucky heather.

Equally misguided, suggests Douglas, is a tendency to view Britain’s uplands as existing outside history, politics, culture and even time itself. The truth is that mountains have shaped much of our island story. When the Romans arrived from mainland Europe in the first century AD, they found that low-lying southern England, with its fertile soil and gentle hillocks, quickly rolled over and signed up to the new order. The craggy north, meanwhile, stood aloof – and you can still see evidence of this bifurcated response in the landscape today. Go to a Roman ruin in the south or east of the country, and chances are that it is the remnants of a country estate or, at the very least, a handsome villa. Head to the high north and you will find yourself scrambling over the remains of a garrison or high brick wall aimed at keeping uplanders away from the good stuff.

And yet … it frequently turns out that it was precisely in those cold, difficult and, above all, lofty places that actual treasure lay. The Romans eventually overcame their fear of heights to start mining lead in Wanlockhead, which at more than 400 metres remains Scotland’s highest village. A thousand years later and the Norman invaders, who had initially given the rocky spine of England a wide berth, set up shop in the Peak District and insisted on taking a cut of the handsome profits that arose from local lead mining.

Douglas suggests that the best way to think of this ceaseless push and pull between the central lowlands and the marginal uplands is as a kind of internal colonialism. For millennia, Britain’s high places have been ransacked for their raw materials. Perhaps the most poignant example in this book is the story of the Elan valley, a beautiful stretch of land in the mountains of rural mid-Wales. In the early 19th century the poet Percy Shelley had roamed over his uncle’s Radnorshire estate, entranced to have found his own version of Wordsworth and Coleridge’s Lake District.

But in 1896, the valley was dammed and flooded in order to create a vast reservoir from which Birmingham might draw an everlasting supply of cheap and clean drinking water. It was part of the MP Joseph Chamberlain’s radical programme to clear England’s second city of cholera and dysentery by building a 73-mile aqueduct from the Welsh mountains to the Midlands plateau. This necessitated the village of Nantgwyllt, complete with church and surrounding farms, disappearing permanently under water.

The compulsory purchase of the Elan valley carries echoes of the earlier Highland clearances, during which tenant farmers in Sutherland, Argyll and Inverness-shire were ordered off the land to make way for the infinitely more profitable sheep. Many of these evicted crofters, just like the Radnorshire farmers 150 years later, were obliged to emigrate as far as the US to find a place to build a stable home.

Yet it would be doomy and defeatist to suggest that the uplands have exclusively been places of passive trauma. Douglas does a good job at identifying those times throughout history when Britain’s high places demonstrated a culture of determined resistance. There are the Jacobite rebellions of 1715 and 1745 when Highlanders loyal to the Stuart cause swept down from their mountain fastness in an attempt to overthrow the newly installed Hanoverians. This tartan army got as far as Derby, only 110 miles from London, before being forced to turn back.

Douglas has not, in truth, found out anything new about the ancient uplands, but he has knitted his sources into a deft survey, going all the way from the tectonic plates of prehistory to today, when the chief concern is southern second-homers driving up the prices for young locals. One delight of his capacious, looping narrative is the room it leaves for delightful cameos by remarkable individuals, including several women.

There is Janet Lapworth, the daughter of a Galashiels schoolteacher, who in the 1870s sewed her geologist husband a special waistcoat incorporating rows of pockets on the front into which he could sort his specimens on the fly. Or Hannah Mitchell, who grew up on a hard-scrabble tenant farm with a view of Kinder Scout, the highest point in the Peak District, and developed a love of rambling to offset the constricted conditions of her own impoverished life. Mitchell’s determination to walk off her troubles led to her becoming a suffragette, a JP and a campaigner for social justice.

My favourite uplander, though, remains Queen Victoria. As a young girl she gorged on the highly confected Highland novels of Walter Scott. Now that Jacobitism was safely defeated, it was delightful to imagine a Highlands full of craggily handsome men in kilts ready to come a lady’s rescue, even if that lady happened to be a Protestant Hanoverian princess. When she bought Balmoral in 1852, the queen was not initially much interested in venturing far. But with the death of Albert she was persuaded to undertake the occasional excursion up famous peaks including Lochnagar and Ben Macdui. Here was the beginning of what the 20th-century novelist George Scott-Moncrieff memorably called “Balmorality”. It was a view of the uplands, spruced up and watered down, best seen on a biscuit tin.

entries.title: Underdogs by Louise Powell review – a powerful debut with plenty of northern soul

entries.content:
The adjoining villages of Easington and Easington Colliery in the coalfields of east Durham make the perfect case study of the shift from England’s industrial boomtime to terminal decline. Twenty miles from a major town or city, they’ve been left to languish ever since Thatcher went to war with the industry that made them. If you want to understand why the white working class feel abandoned today, go to Easington Colliery and its surrounding villages.

It’s this community that Middlesbrough-born writer Louise Powell brings to life in a powerful debut set in the world of greyhound racing, or “flapping”. Underdogs is an utterly authentic depiction of an England that’s overlooked, but still very much alive. Pigeon lofts and flat caps, meat raffles and social clubs – all still exist, just very rarely in 21st-century novels.

Ten-year-old George Wheatley and his broken father Reg, both grieving the loss of George’s mother, who died two years earlier, are drawn into the dog-track culture by charismatic ex-miner Bertie, who despite the “half-pint of black phlegm he hawked up off his lungs every mornin’” decides not to pursue an incapacity benefit claim as he can make better money rinsing out the various illegal bookmakers by racing his dogs. When the bookies refuse to take Bertie’s bets he ropes in those down on their luck to race his dogs for him, and hands over his bitch Goldie, “twenny-nine kilo of muscles coiled like springs … a Ferrari of an engine in her fawn chest and a nose that could been made by Concorde”. Scores of those on the breadline have benefited from Bertie’s hustle.

The love that George feels for Goldie is matched only by his need to survive in an uncompromising adult world where the greatest threat comes from aggrieved bookmaker Baz, who has designs on their prized canine charge. Powell is strongest when describing the details of track life, a seemingly simple pursuit given a dark edge by the high-stakes money changing hands and further complicated by the treatment of these graceful creatures who are bred and discarded for human amusement and profit.

That the novel is set in 1998 is significant; all of County Durham’s pits had finally closed, but major regeneration investment was on its way from local boy Tony Blair, with his talk of “regional task forces” and “enterprise zones”. Old slag piles were soon to became nature reserves and pithead monuments. A bright new future was promised, though it’s barely glimpsed here; today Easington has one of the whitest demographics in the country (currently 98.4%), and was the place worst hit by 2025 disability allowance cuts.

Here, then, is a hard-scratch existence based around family alliances and power struggles in the dying days of an analogue world, where scars received from police truncheons at Orgreave are shown and shared, and where premature death stalks the terraced streets. George and Reg emerge as tender and quietly heroic; the father’s grief for his lost wife is almost overwhelming at times, as are the reminders of George’s malnutrition. This is real first-world poverty, as it still exists today. During the second world war British-based fascist William Joyce, better known as Lord Haw-Haw, remarked that “the people of Easington will be eating greyhounds, not raising them”; he sorely underestimated just how much the English love their dogs, and it’s no coincidence that Powell’s descriptions of the greyhound’s meals are more mouthwatering than anything father and son eat.

North-east writers of literary fiction have always had plenty to sing about, but not much in the way of support from the publishing industry; “too bleak” and “too northern” are words familiar to many of us from the region. Given the rich cultural tradition of storytelling and folk song, always told in distinctively melodic vernacular voices, this still feels like an oversight. With recent novels from Eliza Clark, Glen James Brown, Jessica Andrews and Lucy Rose all finding critical favour, it’s clear that there are infinite Englands in existence. And as Underdogs movingly demonstrates, it’s these untold stories that need to be on the page – now more than ever.

Benjamin Myers’s most recent novel is Jesus Christ Kinski (Bloomsbury).
